title: Where words turn back
hookLine: the Taittiriya says words and mind turn back from Brahman, which is why Hindus can give God a thousand names and call none of them the whole
carry: brahman is beyond words; names only point
last: AT THE CENTER OF YOU IS ANANDA, JOY.

cards: Shankara, the great Vedanta teacher, tells a story. A student named Baskali came to the sage Bahva and said, teach me Brahman. Bahva said, learn it, friend, and fell silent.
Baskali asked again. Silence. A third time: sir, please.
And Bahva said, I am teaching you, but you don't follow. This self is silence. It sounds like a riddle.
It's also the best commentary on a verse in today's chapter of the Taittiriya, which has spent pages mapping the layers of a person, and right in the middle of the map, stops and admits something.

teach.h: WORDS SET OUT, AND TURN BACK.
teach.b: Here's the verse in Sanskrit: yato vaco nivartante aprapya manasa saha. From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having reached it.
Then the second half: the one who knows the bliss of Brahman is never afraid. The picture in nivartante is turning around, coming home. Words set out toward Brahman and come back without arriving.

teach.h: THE MIND TURNS BACK WITH THEM.
teach.b: The mind goes with them, and comes back too. Notice the text doesn't say Brahman is nothing, or that the search is pointless. And it doesn't throw words away.
The very next lines go straight on to the next layer, the self made of understanding. The Upanishad keeps talking, carefully, about the thing it says talk can't hold. That's how a signpost works.
The sign isn't the town, but it tells you which way to walk. Here's a big Hindu teaching in one verse. Brahman, the reality behind everything, can't be boxed by any word or picture.

teach.h: A THOUSAND NAMES, AND NONE IS THE WHOLE.
teach.b: That's why Hindus can call God by a thousand names and many forms, Shiva, Vishnu, the Goddess, and still say no single name is the whole.
Many teachers read the names and images the way this verse reads words: true pointers, not the town.
And then the promise about fear.
The text says, a little later in the chapter, that fear comes when a person makes even a small gap, a sense of separation, inside this. Know the bliss, and there's no gap to be afraid of.

how: This verse is often chanted in Vedanta classes and recitations of the Taittiriya's second chapter, the Brahmanandavalli, and teachers use it to explain why Brahman is pointed to rather than described.

o: they turn back: words and mind, not reaching it
they fall silent forever, giving up
they go forward until they reach the goal

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: the one who knows the bliss

s: the verse means the Upanishad stops talking about Brahman
it keeps teaching, carefully. words point; they just can't capture.
the verse appears twice in the Taittiriya's second chapter
once closing the section on the self made of mind, and again near the chapter's end.
the text links fear to a sense of a gap or separation
fear comes when a person makes even a small gap within it.

games.q: words set out to reach Brahman and come back without arriving. what does the Taittiriya do next?
o: falls silent for the rest of the chapter.
keeps teaching, while admitting words can't hold it.
games.why: the next lines go right on to describe the self made of understanding. the text points with words while saying words turn back.

practice: Pick one sound in the room, a fan, traffic, your own breath, and notice how fast the mind names it; then let the name go and stay with the sound itself, before the label.
When a word arrives, and it will, let it turn back on its own, and return to just hearing, the moment before the word.

wordCard.voice: Nivartante, they turn back. Yato vaco nivartante: the Taittiriya's way of saying Brahman's bliss can be known but not captured in speech.

orig.note: Sanskrit: "from which words turn back." ni + vṛt, to turn back, return.

carryVoice: Your line: brahman is beyond words; names only point. Like Bahva's silence, the verse teaches by turning back. See you tomorrow.
